title: Don't Be a Sucker (1947): how prejudice divided Germany
desc: Don't Be a Sucker is a 1947 U.S. War Department film. It opens on an American street, where a speaker selling a pamphlet turns a crowd against its neighbours, then follows an older man's account of Berlin in 1932: how the Nazis used prejudice as a weapon to divide Germany, what they promised five young men in one crowd, and what those promises came to. Everything said here comes from the film's own narration and dialogue; lines quoted from the film are read in a second voice. The narration voice is synthetic; the archival film is unaltered. Source: U.S. War Department, Educational Film E.F. 6, public domain.

title: When the Government Had Too Many Legal Voices
desc:
Suppose two offices speak for the same government but approach a legal question differently. Both may have expertise. Both may believe their position protects the public business entrusted to them. Yet a court still needs to know what the United States is asking it to do. This episode examines the historical problem behind that situation. Our focus is not the financial administration of courts, which belongs to a different institutional history. It is the coordination of government litigation and the emergence of the solicitor general. The analytical question is how a government transforms several legal perspectives into a position that can be presented responsibly. We will distinguish the creation of an office from the development of its authority, and an official tradition from proof that every individual decision lived up to it.

Original audio-only analytical episode for the Liber Copia podcast. Independently researched; no reading, close adaptation or cover art from any published book.

title: Timbuktu After 1591 and the Survival of Learning
desc:
The Moroccan invasion of fifteen ninety-one is a major turning point in Timbuktu's history. It is not an instruction to imagine that every book vanished or every intellectual activity ended at once. This episode asks how we should understand disruption in a city whose surviving manuscripts preserve a much longer history. Our starting point is the University of Cape Town's Tombouctou Manuscripts Project, read alongside the Library of Congress catalogue of texts from regional collections. We will distinguish political change, the movement of scholars, the loss of particular libraries, and the later survival of written work. These events belong together, but they do not operate on one identical clock. The analytical challenge is to recognise a serious rupture without making continuity invisible, or turning continuity into a denial of the damage.

Original audio-only analytical episode for the Liber Copia podcast. Independently researched; no reading, close adaptation or cover art from any published book.
